headline: Senate FY2027 farm spending draft funds hemp, keeps 11 December THC cap
dek: As the first federal hemp limit starts 12 November, the Senate's FY2027 farm and FDA draft adds 30% for USDA hemp oversight but leaves the 11 December cap in place.
key_points: The Senate Appropriations Committee released its FY2027 agriculture and FDA bill on 10 November, with $27.3 billion in discretionary spending and $12.996 million for USDA's Hemp Production Program, up from $10 million.
The committee's explanatory statement asks the FDA for an enforcement plan on cannabinoid foods within 90 days of enactment and a report on barriers to botanical chronic-pain drugs within 270 days.

Nothing in the draft changes the federal hemp dates: products with cannabinoids the plant cannot make lose hemp status on 12 November, and the 0.4 mg per-container total-THC cap follows on 11 December.
The same 11 December date is when the stopgap law funding the government expires, so any hemp delay would most likely ride on the next funding deal.
body: The first piece of the federal rewrite of hemp takes effect on Thursday, 12 November 2026: from that day, products containing cannabinoids that the cannabis plant cannot naturally produce, such as THC-O, are no longer hemp under federal law. Two days earlier, the Senate Appropriations Committee released the bill that would fund the Department of Agriculture and the Food and Drug Administration for fiscal 2027. It is the first spending text of the new cycle to touch hemp, and it offers the industry money for farming and research but no relief on the shelf.

The draft keeps the bigger change on schedule. On 11 December, the new federal definition of hemp takes full effect, including a cap of 0.4 milligrams of total THC, and similar cannabinoids, per container. That would remove most hemp-derived THC drinks, gummies and flower from general retail nationwide unless Congress acts first. The committee's text does not move that date.
## What the Senate draft does for hemp

The bill would provide $27.3 billion in discretionary funding for USDA, FDA and related agencies, according to the committee and Bloomberg Government. In its explanatory statement, the committee sets $12.996 million for USDA's Hemp Production Program in fiscal 2027, up from $10 million in fiscal 2026, an increase of just under 30%. USAHAA, a hemp trade group, notes the committee summary describes that increase as requested by the administration. The program pays for federal oversight of hemp production.

The research language is broader. The committee tells USDA's Agricultural Research Service to keep funding hemp breeding and genetic work at no less than this year's level, including newer breeding and gene-editing techniques, and to study how hemp fits into existing crop, processing and marketing systems. It directs ARS to build and maintain a hemp germplasm repository at its Plant Genetics Resources Research Unit, noting that the country's public hemp seed collection was destroyed in the 1980s. The statement says the committee sees emerging market potential for hemp and hemp-based products.

The bill itself repeats a long-standing rider, Section 737, that bars federal funds from being used to block the transport, processing, sale or use of hemp grown under federal law. As USAHAA points out, the same rider sat in last year's spending law, Public Law 119-37, which is the law that rewrote the hemp definition. It protects hemp as the law defines it, and that definition is what is narrowing.
> The Senate wants more hemp in the field and less of it in the snack aisle, and this draft funds both halves of that sentence.

The statement's food section reads as a warning to the consumer side of the industry. The committee says it remains concerned by the growth of food products containing plant-derived or other cannabinoids, because no cannabinoid is approved as a food additive. It cites the FDA's more than 110 warning letters to cannabinoid sellers since 2018, encourages the agency to work with other federal agencies and the states on a plan to coordinate enforcement, and directs it to report back within 90 days of enactment on protecting consumers from adulterated foods in interstate commerce.

Paired with the 11 December cap, that is a signal that Senate appropriators see enforcement, not a new regulatory lane, as the next step for intoxicating hemp foods and drinks. The FDA has already missed the 10 February deadline in last year's law to publish lists of cannabinoids and related compounds, as we reported on 9 November, and those lists are what the 12 November exclusion depends on.

On medicine, the tone is warmer. In a section on chronic pain, the committee notes the FDA's draft guidance on non-opioid painkillers and points to late-stage European trials of botanical, cannabinoid-based pain therapies that could lead to approvals there. It urges the FDA to give such products timely, science-based reviews, taking account of patient-reported outcomes and the potential to cut opioid use, and directs the agency to report within 270 days of enactment on scientific or regulatory gaps that hold back botanical pain drugs, including how it could draw on evidence from European and other regulators.

None of this is binding yet. The bill is a committee draft that still needs markup, a Senate vote and agreement with the House. Its report language would take effect only through a final appropriations law.

The timing matters more than the text. The stopgap law signed on 2 September, Public Law 119-103, funds the government through 11 December, the same day the hemp cap takes effect, according to the Congressional Research Service as cited by USAHAA. Congress must pass full-year bills or another stopgap before then. That makes the year-end funding package the most likely vehicle for any further hemp delay or a regulatory framework, and also the moment when one could be left out.

States are not waiting. Missouri's law treating intoxicating hemp products as marijuana and Illinois' Hemp Act both start on 12 November, as we reported on 11 November, so some sellers face state limits before the federal cap arrives.

Watch the Senate committee's markup schedule for amendments that would add a hemp delay or a regulated lane for hemp-derived THC. The shape of the next stopgap, due by 11 December, will decide whether the federal cap lands on time. And watch for the FDA's overdue cannabinoid lists, which would show which compounds fall outside federal hemp from Thursday.
